stem: A 69-year-old man who travels seasonally for construction labor was identified with a chronic cough during a mobile outreach clinic that periodically visits labor camps and informal settlements to screen high-risk, marginalized populations for TB, part of a standing national program activity. He has advanced COPD, previously diagnosed, and uses a bronchodilator inhaler that he often cannot afford to refill. He had been coughing for well over three months, attributing it entirely to his COPD. He was diagnosed with drug-sensitive pulmonary TB six weeks ago and started on treatment, directly observed at the camp's health post. Sputum smear remains positive at today's 2-month assessment, and he reports feeling more breathless than his usual COPD baseline. Vitals: oxygen saturation 90% on room air (his documented COPD baseline is 95%), respiratory rate 27/min. Initial chest imaging showed extensive bilateral cavitary disease.

patient.social_history: Lives in labor camps/informal settlements while traveling for seasonal work; inconsistent access to his COPD medication
patient.presenting_complaint: Follow-up at 2 months of TB treatment: persistent positive sputum smear, breathlessness beyond his known COPD baseline
patient.duration: 12+ weeks prior to diagnosis (delayed presentation); now 2 months into treatment
patient.exam_findings: SpO2 90% room air (baseline 95%), respiratory rate 27/min; extensive bilateral cavitary disease on chest X-ray at diagnosis
patient.prior_treatment: 2 months of standard first-line anti-TB therapy to date; no prior TB treatment before this episode

distractors: His advanced COPD proposed as sufficient explanation for the breathlessness and low oxygen saturation without considering a change from his documented baseline
Inconsistent access to his COPD medication proposed as the primary driver of his current symptoms
The persistent positive smear at 2 months attributed entirely to his severe underlying lung disease impairing sputum clearance, rather than a slow treatment response
ntep_correct_actions: Leave the decision to extend the continuation phase for this slow bacteriological responder to the treating physician's case-by-case clinical judgment, rather than applying a fixed extension rule.

Recognize that this patient's case was appropriately identified through routine active case-finding targeted at marginalized/high-risk populations (labor camps and informal settlements), consistent with standing national program policy rather than a threshold-gated activity.

Escalate or refer this patient to a higher-tier facility now, since his oxygen saturation (90%, below his own known baseline) and respiratory rate (27/min) each independently meet the quantified red-flag criteria that mandate referral.
who_correct_actions: Do not extend the regimen based on this patient's positive 2-month smear alone; the standard regimen is fixed-duration, and extension in response to bacteriological non-conversion is not recommended.

Treat this kind of active case-finding as conditionally appropriate only where the local TB prevalence has been shown to meet the recommended threshold (approximately 0.5% or higher), rather than as a routine activity applied irrespective of a demonstrated local prevalence.

Base the decision to refer or escalate his care on individualized clinical judgment of his hypoxia and tachypnea; there is no WHO-specified quantified threshold mandating escalation, only a general direction toward decentralized care where it is safe.
us_correct_actions: Extend the continuation phase by an additional 3 months (9 months total) given the cavitary lesion on his initial chest radiograph combined with the positive smear/culture at completion of 2 months of therapy.

Attribute his case identification to contact investigation following a known index case rather than population-level active case-finding; a routine mobile outreach screening of this kind is not the primary case-finding model in this framework.

Base the decision to hospitalize or refer this patient on individualized clinical judgment regarding his hypoxia and tachypnea, since there is no codified, quantified, nationally standardized threshold-based triage protocol in this framework either.
critical_error_conditions: Attributing the drop in oxygen saturation below his own documented COPD baseline entirely to his chronic lung disease and taking no action in response to today's vitals
expected_divergence_points: Whether continuation-phase extension for slow bacteriological response is a matter of physician discretion, discouraged under a fixed-duration regimen, or governed by a specific cavitation-plus-culture-based expert rule

Whether this patient's outreach-based active case-finding pathway among a marginalized population reflects standard, unconditional national program policy or is only appropriate where a threshold local prevalence is demonstrated
Whether his current vital-sign abnormalities trigger a mandatory, quantified escalation/referral or are left to individualized clinical judgment
